text: Click Start the tutorial. You've just opened a little electronics repair shop. This walkthrough fixes your first job with you , a desk lamp that will not turn on , one step at a time, then shows you around the office. Takes about 10 minutes. You can skip it now or at any point, and replay it later from the Help button.
Click Start next to Robin T. This is the office: customers wait here, and so do your supplies, orders and money. Robin T has brought in a lamp.

Read the ticket, then click Next. The ticket says what the customer noticed: completely dead. Always start with the symptom. Stuck later? Need a nudge? on the ticket gives a hint, and the Service sheet shows the board's blocks and test points.
Click Customer adapter. The customer's own adapter powers the lamp. Watch the status lines under the buttons: nothing lights up. Now let's find out why.

Click test point 1 with the red probe. The multimeter is set to volts, and we have clipped its black probe to ground , test point 5, for you. The Black ground button does that any time. The red probe goes on the raw input, where the adapter's power arrives.
Click test point 2. test point 1 reads about 12 V: power is getting into the board. test point 2 is the 12 V rail a little further along, after the protection parts.

Click Off. test point 2 reads 0 V! Power gets in at test point 1 but is lost before test point 2. The only part between them is the fuse, F 1, so let's test it. Resistance, continuity and diode tests only make sense with the power off.
Click the continuity mode on the multimeter. In continuity mode the meter beeps when the two probes are connected through almost nothing: perfect for checking a fuse.
First, Left-click one end of F 1 , red probe. Then, Right-click the other end of F 1 , black probe. A good fuse beeps and reads close to 0 ohms.

First, Choose Soldering , key 3, later: click Rework at the microscope. Then, Click the fuse F 1 on the board. No beep, and the meter reads O L, an open circuit: the fuse has blown. Found it! The part card that opens on the left has the button that takes you to the microscope.
Click Flux , or press 3. Welcome to the microscope. The yellow hint box on the right always suggests the next move. First, flux: it lets the heat flow and the old solder run.
Click or hold on every marked pad , clicking again adds more flux. Flux on both ends of the fuse helps the heat flow and the old solder run.
Click Wick , or press 2. The wick is a copper braid: heated, it soaks the molten solder up off the pad.

Hold the wick on each marked joint until the solder is gone. Warning. Heat kills pads. A pad that stays molten for about ten seconds, or gets far above 320 degrees, burns and lifts off the board, and the repair is ruined. Work in short bursts, watch the pad heat bar, and let go before it fills. Press and hold on a joint: the iron heats through the braid and the solder runs into it. The pad should end up bare copper. If the wick end turns silver, cut it off with C; if the flux is gone, add more.
Click Tweezers , or press 4. The tweezers pick parts up and set them down.
Click the fuse to pick it up with the tweezers. The solder is off, so nothing holds the fuse down any more.
Press Delete on your keyboard to bin the fuse in the tweezers. The blown fuse is no use to anyone any more.
Click New beside Fuse 1A fast in the Parts tray. It comes out of your stock and lands in the tweezers.
Click the empty footprint to set the fuse down on the pads. It only counts if it sits on both pads.
Click Flux , or press 3. Flux again, so the solder flows into the new joints.
Click or hold on every marked pad , clicking again adds more flux. Fresh flux on both pads helps the new solder flow.
Click Iron , or press 1. The iron heats the pad, and the solder wire melts into the joint.

Look at the Joints section on the right, then click Got it. The panel has been scrolled to Joints. Each pad shows its solder bar , about half full = a good joint, no blob, its temperature, and a Pad heat bar: if that one fills, the pad burns off the board.

Press and hold the mouse button on the marked pad until the readout says MOLTEN. Watch the pad heat bar, and let go before it fills. Hold the iron's tip on the pad , hover it to read its temperature. Solder melts at about 220 degrees, so MOLTEN appears long before the pad is in danger. Keep the pad under about 320 degrees.

Keep the iron on the pad , still MOLTEN, and hold Space for 1 to 2 seconds. Watch the pad heat bar, and let go before it fills. Holding Space feeds solder wire into the molten joint. In the Joints panel the solder bar should reach about half , 50 percent,: a solid joint without a blob. Then let go and lift the iron.

Press and hold the mouse button on the marked pad until the readout says MOLTEN. Watch the pad heat bar, and let go before it fills. Hold the iron's tip on the pad , hover it to read its temperature. Solder melts at about 220 degrees, so MOLTEN appears long before the pad is in danger. Keep the pad under about 320 degrees.

Keep the iron on the pad , still MOLTEN, and hold Space for 1 to 2 seconds. Watch the pad heat bar, and let go before it fills. Holding Space feeds solder wire into the molten joint. In the Joints panel the solder bar should reach about half , 50 percent,: a solid joint without a blob. Then let go and lift the iron.
Click Flux , or press 3. A hot-air reflow melts both joints together so the solder flows evenly and the fuse pulls itself straight. It needs fresh flux first.
Click or hold on every marked pad , clicking again adds more flux. Fresh flux lets the solder flow evenly during the reflow.
Click Hot air , or press 5. Hot air heats the whole part evenly, with no tip touching the pads.

Hold the mouse button and sweep back and forth over both joints until they read 300 to 320 degrees, then let go. Watch the pad heat bar, and let go before it fills. Keep the nozzle moving over both joints at the same time. The flux bubbles as it heats. Hover a pad for its temperature. When both are about 300 to 320 degrees, stop: any longer and the pads start to burn.
Click Liquid , or press 6. The flux has done its job and what is left is sticky. Let go of the hot air first, then pick the Liquid tool to clean it off.
Make sure Cleaning liquid says Isopropyl alcohol , I P A, then click Next. The Cleaning liquid selector decides what the Liquid tool applies. For flux, use I P A , isopropyl alcohol.
Hold the Liquid tool on each marked joint until the flux dissolves into the I P A. Keep it wet until the flux melts into the I P A: the liquid turns cloudy and yellowish.
Click Brush , or press 7. The brush loosens the dissolved flux. Only scrub while the pad is wet.
Scrub back and forth over each marked joint until the flux ovals disappear. If the I P A dries before you finish, pick the Liquid tool and add a little more.
Click Wipe , or press 8. The wipe lifts the dissolved flux away. One side has already dried, leaving white residue marks: that is what happens when I P A evaporates before you wipe.
Drag the wipe across the joint that is still wet. Save the side that is still wet first.
Click Liquid , or press 6. The white marks are dried flux. Do not scrape them: dissolve them again with I P A.
Hold the Liquid tool on the marked residue until it turns liquid again. When the white residue goes cloudy and wet, it can be wiped.
Click Wipe , or press 8. Now wipe it away, quickly, before it dries again.
Drag the wipe over the marked joints until they are clean. The pads should end up clean and shiny.

Click Done to put the board back on the bench. Clean, shiny joints. Messed up , a lifted pad, a blob, a crooked fuse? Click Undo all instead: the board goes back exactly as it was when you sat down, and you can try again.

Click Undo all, then confirm. Too much heat for too long: a copper pad burned and peeled off the board. A fuse soldered to it would not connect, and the lamp would stay dead. No harm done in the tutorial. The board goes back exactly as it was when you sat down, and you can try again. This time, work in short bursts and watch the Pad heat bar.
Click Customer adapter. Back on the bench. Time to test it the way the customer will.
Press and hold the lamp button , or hold Space. The lamp should light up. If it doesn't, re-check your joints at the microscope.
Click Case: open. It lights up, so the fuse is fixed! The lamp is still out of its case, so let's put it back together.
Click Close it up for me. This is the teardown bench, where you take cases apart and put them back together, screw by screw.
Click Done. All screwed back together.
Click Return to customer. The lamp is fixed and closed up. Time to hand it back.
Click Return to Robin T. Robin tests it at home. Good work gets paid and builds your reputation; sloppy joints can come back later as free warranty repairs.
Click Tour the office. You found the fault, swapped the fuse like a pro and got paid. Next, a quick tour of the office, where you run the business side of the shop.
The Overview tab is your shop at a glance: today's alerts , low supplies, rent due, deliveries on the way, profit and loss for today and the week, and the ledger of every payment in and out.

The Work tab lists the customers waiting and the devices you own , your projects. Click Start to put one on the bench. Customers don't wait forever , after about three days they collect their device unrepaired.

On Supplies & parts you buy what the microscope uses up: solder, flux, wick, I P A, brushes and wipes. Run out and that tool stops working. To buy: click + next to a pack to add it to the Order basket.

Further down is Components in stock: every fuse, resistor, capacitor and chip you have, and what they cost. Use + to add parts to the basket too. In the Order basket, pick a delivery speed and click Place order , it arrives on a later morning. Cheap parts can also be rush-bought one at a time from the microscope's parts tray; expensive chips are special order.
The Store-room holds donor boards: repairs you gave up on and parts-only devices you bought. Pull parts off them , retimers, screens, programmed chips , when a job needs one and nobody sells it new.

Equipment sells new capabilities: an ESR meter, an oscilloscope, a thermal camera, microscope upgrades, test consoles for cartridges, and better iron tips and hot-air nozzles. Choose tips and nozzles in the microscope's kit selectors.

The Marketplace sells broken devices. Buy one with Buy for $…: a normal listing goes to Work Your projects to repair and sell on for profit; a parts only listing goes to the store-room as a donor to stockpile parts. Need one exact chip? Search online for a donor of that device at the top.
Advertising brings in more customers each day, and people who find you through ads accept slightly higher quotes. It's billed every night, so start small.
When you're done for the day, click End day. Tonight's bills get paid , electricity, rent every 7 days, advertising, orders arrive, and new customers come in the next morning.
Want a fresh start? The Career card on the Overview tab has ⟲ Start a new career: back to day 1 with a new shop, starting cash and a starter pack of parts. It wipes the current save.
Forgot something? Click the Help button at the top right any time , it explains the controls and has Play the tutorial to run this walkthrough again. That's everything. Good luck with the shop!
